newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks not seen at start of major reversal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks not seen at start of major reversal.

text.p: U.S. stocks might see some followthrough selling early next week but do not appear to be at the start of a major reversal, analysts said Friday.

Stocks sold off sharply spooked by a steep rise in long-term interest rates, but there has not been the sort of fundamemental shift in the scenarios for interest rates or corporate profits to cripple Wall Street's bull market, they said.
The Dow was off about 115 points, or 1.4 percent, at 8072 in late trading Friday after falling more than 200 in the session.
The downdraft was triggered by selloff in the bond market that drove the yield on the 30-year bond to 6.64 percent in late trading Friday from Thursday's close at 6.53 percent.
Analysts said that greater concern about growth in the U.S. economy -- and subsequent inflation -- would weigh on bonds in the near term.
But significant damage to stocks and bonds were unlikely unless inflation shows signs of kicking in, which it has yet to do, analysts said.

"The bond market continues to have an over-sensitivity to growth because it concludes growth creates inflation," said Thomas McManus, chief market strategist at NatWest Securities. "I don't think inflation is a problem."
McManus said that the long bond yield could rise to 6.75 percent and the Standard & Poor's 500 dip to 900 as part of the current pullback, although he added stocks "could stabilize at any time."
The S&P 500 was off 16 points, or 1.7 percent at 935.01 in late trading Friday.
The Dow hit a record closing high of 8259.31 on Wednesday, up 29 percent from its closing low of 6391.69 for the year hit April 11.
The rise has left stocks with very little room for news that does not fit into the "perfect world" scenario of steady growth and low inflation, analysts said.
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist Josephthal Lyon & Ross, likened Friday's selloff to a child realizing the "Tooth Fairy" does not exist.
"It's not the end of the world," he said.

But analysts said there were some warning signs in Friday's action, including the widespread nature of the selloff. Losing issues outnumber gainers by a five-to-one ratio on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The breadth was just awful today," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.

While Acuff called Friday's move "healthy profit taking" following the stocks' recent rise, he said investors should expect further volatility as traders give extra scrutiny to upcoming economic data, including Wednesday's retail sales and producer price data and Thursday's consumer price numbers.
The question will be whether a major reversal of the recent trend of declining interest rates will set in, said Robert Walberg, chief equity analysts at Briefing.Com.

If the long-bond yield holds below 7.00 percent, a downturn of more than 500 points from the Dow peak is unlikely, Walberg said. "But if we're seeing a significant sea change in the bond market, it could get ugly for stocks."

But some analysts expressed confidence investors would continue their habit of using selloffs as buying opportunities. "I think they buy the dips," said William LeFevre, senior market analyst at Ehrenkrantz King Nussbaum.
